# Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on behalf of Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya

**Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on behalf of Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya** (Communication 276/2003), commonly known as the **Endorois case**, is a landmark decision issued by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) in 2010 . The ruling addressed the expulsion of the Endorois people, an indigenous pastoralist community, from their ancestral lands around Lake Bogoria in Kenya to create a game reserve .

The decision is legally significant for two primary reasons: it was the first time the African Commission recognized the existence of indigenous peoples in Africa with rights over traditionally owned land, and it was the first ruling by an international tribunal to find a violation of the right to development . The Commission found the Government of Kenya in violation of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, specifically regarding the rights to religious practice, property, culture, the free disposition of natural resources, and development . Despite the ruling being adopted by the African Union in 2010, implementation of the Commission's recommendations remains limited as of 2025 .

## Background

### The Endorois People
The Endorois are a semi-nomadic, pastoralist indigenous community of approximately 60,000 people who have historically inhabited the Lake Bogoria area in the Rift Valley Province of Kenya . They are often classified as a sub-group of the Tugen, who are part of the larger Kalenjin ethnic group, though they maintain a distinct cultural identity . Their livelihood relies heavily on livestock herding, and their culture is inextricably linked to the land surrounding Lake Bogoria, which they consider sacred . The community utilizes the lake's hot springs for religious ceremonies and the surrounding areas for grazing and traditional herbal medicine .

### Eviction and Domestic Litigation
In 1973, the Kenyan government established the Lake Hannington Game Reserve (renamed Lake Bogoria Game Reserve in 1978) . To facilitate this, the government evicted the Endorois community from their ancestral lands . The eviction process began in the 1970s and continued into the 1980s .

The Endorois alleged that these evictions occurred without proper prior consultation or adequate compensation . The displacement forced the community into semi-arid areas, resulting in the loss of livestock and disrupting their traditional way of life . The community was also denied access to the game reserve for grazing or religious purposes, except at the discretion of the Game Reserve Authority .

In the 1990s, the Endorois Welfare Council (EWC) attempted to seek redress through the Kenyan domestic legal system . They filed a case in the High Court of Kenya, arguing that the eviction was illegal and violated their constitutional rights. However, the High Court dismissed the case in 2002 . The court ruled that the land was "Trust Land" managed by the County Council for the benefit of the residents, but that the creation of the game reserve superseded the community's customary rights . The court further stated that Kenyan law did not recognize collective land rights based on cultural claims . Following the exhaustion of domestic remedies, the Centre for Minority Rights Development (CEMIRIDE) and Minority Rights Group International (MRG) filed a complaint with the ACHPR on behalf of the Endorois in 2003 .

## Proceedings before the African Commission

The communication (complaint) was declared admissible by the African Commission in 2005 . The complainants argued that the expulsion of the Endorois from their land violated the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, specifically:
* **Article 8:** Right to practice religion.
* **Article 14:** Right to property.
* **Article 17:** Right to culture.
* **Article 21:** Right to free disposition of natural resources.
* **Article 22:** Right to development .

The Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) submitted an *amicus curiae* brief in support of the Endorois .

The Respondent State (Kenya) argued that the Endorois were not a distinct indigenous group but part of the larger Kalenjin community, and therefore not entitled to special protection as a "people" under the Charter . Kenya further contended that the creation of the game reserve was for the broader public interest, specifically tourism and wildlife conservation, and that the Trust Land system provided adequate legal administration for the land .

## Judgment

In November 2009, during its 46th Ordinary Session, the African Commission issued its ruling, finding the Government of Kenya in violation of Articles 1, 8, 14, 17, 21, and 22 of the African Charter . The decision was formally adopted by the African Union Heads of State Summit in February 2010 .

### Recognition of Indigenous Status
A central aspect of the ruling was the Commission's determination that the Endorois constitute a distinct "people" and an indigenous community . The Commission applied criteria including self-identification, distinct cultural patterns, and a special attachment to ancestral land . This rejected the Kenyan government's argument that all Africans are indigenous and that the Endorois were merely a sub-group without distinct collective rights . This finding established a precedent for the protection of indigenous rights within the African human rights system .

### Right to Property (Article 14)
The Commission ruled that the Endorois' traditional possession of the land was equivalent to state-granted full property title . It found that the "Trust Land" system, which allowed local councils to hold land on behalf of residents, had failed to protect the community's rights . The Commission stated that the encroachment on Endorois land was disproportionate to the public need for a game reserve and that the community had not been adequately compensated .

### Right to Development (Article 22)
The *Endorois case* is widely cited as the first international jurisprudence to find a violation of the Right to Development . The Commission established that development processes must include the "active, free and meaningful participation" of the affected community . It ruled that the Kenyan government failed to obtain the "free, prior, and informed consent" (FPIC) of the Endorois before evicting them . Furthermore, the Commission noted that development should result in the improvement of the community's well-being, whereas the eviction had led to a decline in their welfare .

### Religious and Cultural Rights (Articles 8 and 17)
The ruling recognized that the Endorois' spiritual beliefs and ceremonial practices constituted a religion protected under the Charter . By denying the community unrestricted access to Lake Bogoria (a sacred site) and surrounding areas for religious rituals, the state had violated their freedom of religion . The Commission dismissed the state's argument that access could be regulated or restricted for conservation purposes, stating that the Endorois' presence was not incompatible with conservation .

### Recommendations
The African Commission issued several recommendations to the Government of Kenya to remedy the violations:
1. **Restitution:** Recognize the Endorois' rights of ownership and return their ancestral land .
2. **Access:** Ensure unrestricted access to Lake Bogoria and surrounding sites for religious rites and grazing .
3. **Compensation:** Pay adequate compensation for all losses suffered .
4. **Royalties:** Pay royalties from existing economic activities (tourism and mining) and ensure employment opportunities within the reserve .
5. **Registration:** Grant registration to the Endorois Welfare Council .
6. **Dialogue:** Engage in dialogue with the complainants to implement the recommendations .

## Implementation

Following the 2010 ruling, implementation of the Commission's recommendations has been slow and contentious.

### Initial Response and Task Force
The Kenyan government initially expressed a willingness to comply, and the Endorois Welfare Council was successfully registered, fulfilling one of the recommendations . In 2014, the government established a task force with a one-year mandate to study the decision and guide its implementation . However, the task force's term expired without the release of a public report or significant progress on the ground .

### Status as of 2024–2025
As of 2025, the core recommendations regarding land restitution and compensation remain largely unimplemented .
* **Land Rights:** The Endorois have not been granted legal title to their ancestral lands, and the community continues to face restrictions on access .
* **Compensation:** No comprehensive compensation package has been provided for the historical losses .
* **Continued Displacement:** Reports indicate that members of the Endorois community have faced further displacement risks from related areas, such as the Mochongoi Forest and Mukutani Forest, due to security operations and conservation measures .

In February 2024, the Endorois Welfare Council, alongside the Ogiek community (who won a similar case at the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights), delivered call-to-action letters to the Kenyan Attorney General demanding immediate implementation of the rulings . Civil society organizations, including Minority Rights Group International and ESCR-Net, continue to advocate for the government to honor its obligations under the African Charter .

## Significance
The *Endorois case* is considered a cornerstone of indigenous rights jurisprudence in Africa . It clarified the definition of "peoples" under the African Charter to explicitly include indigenous populations, distinguishing them from the broader population of a state .

The case also set a global precedent regarding the Right to Development. By linking development to the requirement of "free, prior, and informed consent," the Commission established that state development projects cannot legally proceed at the expense of the fundamental rights and well-being of indigenous communities . The ruling has influenced subsequent litigation, including the *Ogiek case* (*African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights v. Kenya*), where the African Court relied on principles established in the Endorois decision .

The Endorois and their struggle for the realization of the right to development
===============================================================================

[Read more](http://www.un-ngls.org/spip.php?article3607)

The Endorois are a pastoralist community of 60,000 indigenous people, who have resided in the Lake Bogoria area of Kenya for the past centuries. Between 1974 and 1979, the Kenyan government forcefully evicted them to create the Lake Bogoria Game Reserve \[and tourism development\]. This not only destructed their material livelihoods, but also disconnected their spiritual connection with their ancestral land. The Endorois lodged a legal appeal in 1998 to the high court of Kenya, but the case was ruled in favor of the government. In 2003,...they took the case to the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights...In 2010, the Commission delivered its landmark decision affirming the violation of the Endorois’ rights and ordered the Kenyan government to restore the Endorois’ access to their ancestral land with compensation.

Kenya: Landmark Ruling on Indigenous Land Rights
================================================

African Human Rights Commission Condemns Expulsion of Endorois People for Tourism Development

[Share this via Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights "Share this via Facebook") [Share this via Bluesky](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights%0Ahttps://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights "Share this via Bluesky") [Share this via X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights&url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights "Share this via X") [Share this via WhatsApp](whatsapp://send?text=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights%20-%20https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights "Share this via WhatsApp") [Share this via Email](mailto:?subject=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights&body=https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights "Share this via Email") More sharing options [Share this via LinkedIn](http://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights&title=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights "Share this via LinkedIn") [Share this via Reddit](http://reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights&title=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights "Share this via Reddit") [Share this via Telegram](https://telegram.me/share/url?url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2010/02/04/kenya-landmark-ruling-indigenous-land-rights&text=Kenya:LandmarkRulingonIndigenousLandRights "Share this via Telegram") [Share this via Printer](https://www.hrw.org/node/238793/printable/print "Share this via Printer")

(New York) - A ruling by the African Commission on Human and People's Rights condemning the expulsion of the Endorois people from their land in Kenya is a major victory for indigenous peoples across Africa, Human Rights Watch, WITNESS, and the Endorois' lawyers said today. The Commission ruled on February 4, 2010 that the Endorois' eviction from their traditional land for tourism development violated their human rights.

The Kenyan government evicted the Endorois people, a traditional pastoralist community, from their homes at Lake Bogoria in central Kenya in the 1970s, to make way for a national reserve and tourist facilities. In the first ruling of an international tribunal to find a violation of the right to development, the Commission found that this eviction, with minimal compensation, violated the Endorois' right as an indigenous people to property, health, culture, religion, and natural resources. It ordered [Kenya](https://www.hrw.org/africa/kenya) to restore the Endorois to their historic land and to compensate them. It is the first ruling to determine who are indigenous peoples in Africa, and what are their rights to land. The case was brought on behalf of the Endorois by [CEMIRIDE](http://www.witness.org/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=511&Itemid=44) and [Minority Rights Group International](http://www.minorityrights.org/7407/trouble-in-paradise/meet-the-endorois.html).

"The Endorois decision, the first of its kind, can help many others across Africa who have been forced from their homes," said Clive Baldwin, senior legal adviser at Human Rights Watch, who was co-counsel for the Endorois in the case while employed with Minority Rights Group International. "The African Commission is clear: the land where the Endorois historically lived is their property and must be returned to them."

Lake Bogoria is considered to have great tourism potential due to its hot springs and abundant wildlife, including one of Africa's largest populations of flamingos. The African Commission accepted the Endorois' evidence that they have lived there since "time immemorial" and the lake was the center of their religion and culture, with their ancestors buried nearby. After being evicted from the fertile land around the lake, the Endorois were forced to congregate on arid land, where many of their cattle died.

They tried unsuccessfully to persuade the Kenyan government, the local authorities, and the Kenyan Wildlife Service to reverse their policy of evicting everyone, including traditional inhabitants, from areas the government designated national parks and reserves. They were also rebuffed when they sought an adequate share of the tourism and revenues generated by the reserve. After Kenyan courts refused to address their case, they brought their case to the African Commission in 2003. As a component of the case, WITNESS and CEMIRIDE collaborated on a landmark use of [video as evidence](http://hub.witness.org/en/RightfulPlace), demonstrating how conditions on the ground breached articles of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, and bringing voices of the Endorois to the Commission.

Violations of land rights, including the rights of the generations of Kenyans displaced through historic and recent evictions, are one of the key unresolved issues in Kenya, which former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan acknowledged in the aftermath of Kenya's electoral violence in 2007-2008. The African Commission found that the Kenyan government has continued to rely on a colonial law that prevented certain communities from holding land outright, and allowed others, such as local authorities, effectively to own their traditional land on "trust" for these Communities. The local authority in Lake Bogoria was able to end the Endorois trust at will and to seize the land.

In the last decade there have been several attempts at comprehensive land reform that would allow for final and fair determination of land ownership and create a system to restore land to those unlawfully evicted or to compensate them. None of these reforms has been completed. While the adoption by the government of a new land policy in August 2009 marks a significant step forward, it still needs to be translated into effective protection on the ground for Kenya's most marginalized.

"This ruling is good for every Kenyan," said Korir Singo'ei, who represented the Endorois while director of CEMIRIDE. "The law that treats some communities as children, unable to own their own land, is a colonial relic that needs to be changed."

The African Commission determined that the Endorois, having a clear historic attachment to particular land, are a distinct indigenous people, a term contested by some African governments who claimed all Africans are indigenous. It also found that the Endorois had property rights over the land they traditionally occupied and used, even though the British and Kenyan authorities had denied them a formal title. In finding a violation of the right to development for the first time the Commission relied on the failure of the Kenyan authorities to respect the right of the Endorois to consent to development, and the failure to provide them adequate compensation for the loss they had suffered, or any benefit from the tourism.

The African Commission had ruled in 2006 against the Kenyan government for allowing a ruby mining company to start illegal mining on another part of the Endorois' land, severely affecting their remaining access to water. Following that ruling, the mining company abandoned its activities.

"The African Commission's ruling makes clear to governments that they must treat indigenous peoples as active stakeholders rather than passive beneficiaries," said Cynthia Morel, who was co-counsel for the Endorois as senior legal adviser with Minority Rights Groups International. "That recognition is a victory for all indigenous peoples across Africa whose existence was largely ignored - both in law and in fact - until today. The ruling spells the beginning of a brighter future."

The Commission requires Kenya to take steps to return the Endorois land and compensate them within three months. Comprehensive reform to bring Kenya's land laws to the standards set by the Commission is vital before the 2012 elections, Human Rights Watch, WITNESS, and the Endorois' lawyers said.

Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group (on behalf of Endorois Welfare Council) / Kenya - 276/03
=================================================================================================================================

Nov 25, 2009

share[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://achpr.au.int/en/decisions-communications/centre-minority-rights-development-kenya-and-minority-rights-group-27603)[](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet/?text=CentreforMinorityRightsDevelopment\(Kenya\)andMinorityRightsGroup\(onbehalfofEndoroisWelfareCouncil\)/Kenya-276/03&url=https://achpr.au.int/en/decisions-communications/centre-minority-rights-development-kenya-and-minority-rights-group-27603)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://achpr.au.int/en/decisions-communications/centre-minority-rights-development-kenya-and-minority-rights-group-27603&title=CentreforMinorityRightsDevelopment\(Kenya\)andMinorityRightsGroup\(onbehalfofEndoroisWelfareCouncil\)/Kenya-276/03&summary=&source=)[](mailto:?subject=CentreforMinorityRightsDevelopment\(Kenya\)andMinorityRightsGroup\(onbehalfofEndoroisWelfareCouncil\)/Kenya-276/03&body=https://achpr.au.int/en/decisions-communications/centre-minority-rights-development-kenya-and-minority-rights-group-27603)[](javascript:void\(0\))

**Recommendations of the African Commission**

In view of the above, the African Commission finds that the Respondent State is in violation of Articles 1, 8, 14, 17, 21 and 22 of the African Charter. The African Commission recommends that the Respondent State:

(a) Recognise rights of ownership to the Endorois and Restitute Endorois ancestral land.

(b) Ensure that the Endorois community has unrestricted access to Lake Bogoria and surrounding sites for religious and cultural rites and for grazing their cattle.

(c) Pay adequate compensation to the community for all the loss suffered.

(d) Pay royalties to the Endorois from existing economic activities and ensure that they benefit from employment possibilities within the reserve.

(e) Grant registration to the Endorois Welfare Committee.

(f) Engage in dialogue with the Complainants for the effective implementation of these recommendations. (g) Report on the implementation of these recommendations within three months from the date of notification.

2\. The African Commission avails its good offices to assist the parties in the implementation of these recommendations.

**Done in Banjul, The Gambia at the 46th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights held from 11th – 25th November 2009.**

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Endorois
Total population
60,000 (2011, est.)
Regions with significant populations
Lake Bogoria (Kenya)
Languages
Endorois variety of Kalenjin languages
Religion
Traditional religion
Related ethnic groups
  • Tugen people
  • Kalenjin people
The **Endorois** are an indigenous people from the area of [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria") in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley "Great Rift Valley") region of Kenya. They are a subgroup of the [Tugen people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tugen_people "Tugen people"), in turn classified as [Kalenjin people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_people "Kalenjin people"). They are a [pastoralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoralism "Pastoralism") group that traditionally herded livestock in Lake Bogoria's [lowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowlands "Lowlands") and the nearby Mochongoi Forest. In Endorois beliefs, their ancestors originated in the forest, and the lake is the spiritual home of living and dead Endorois. They speak a variety of the [Kalenjin languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_languages "Kalenjin languages"). The Endorois lived near [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria") for centuries before the British Empire claimed it as part of the [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony"). Under the British [land ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_ownership "Land ownership") system, the area was entrusted to the government on behalf of the Endorois; a trust system continued under independent [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"). In 1973, the Kenyan government converted the area to a [game reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_reserve "Game reserve"), requiring the relocation of the Endorois. The Endorois Welfare Council (EWC) was created in 1985 and advocated for the Endorois to return to their land. The EWC filed a case with the [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_/(Kenya/) "High Court (Kenya)") in the 1990s, alleging that the removal was illegal, but the court sided with the state. The EWC then filed the [Endorois case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case "Endorois case") with the [African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Commission_on_Human_and_Peoples%27_Rights "African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights"), alleging that the removal had violated their human rights. The commission ruled in favor of the EWC in 2009 and recommended that the government recognise the Endorois community's land claim. As of 2023, the government has not fully granted the Endorois ownership of the land. The Endorois people resided near [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria") since the pre-colonial era,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020500-1) at least as far back as the seventeenth century.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268-2) These lands were around Mochongoi Forest, within the Lakipia Plains.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-Mavenjina-3) Their [land claim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_claim "Land claim") was recognised by nearby communities.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBavikatte2014160Batt2024183-4) The [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") claimed the land of the Endorois as part of the [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011300-5) During this time, the term _Endorois_ referred to a local government area (part of modern-day [Baringo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_County "Baringo County")).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201228-6) Authorities considered this area "the most backward location" in the colony.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201243-7) Authorities as well as the Endorois themselves considered the community a subgroup of the [Tugen people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tugen_people "Tugen people"), the predominant ethnic group of the region.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201228-6) Colonization introduced a system of [land ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_ownership "Land ownership") in which the central government had power over land rights.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012159-8) The Native Lands Trust Board classified the Endorois land as indigenous land,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269-9) placing it under traditional [land tenure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_tenure "Land tenure")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201061-10) and granting the Endorois freedom over their land.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBavikatte2014160-11) The government administered it under the county governments of Baringo and [Koibatek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koibatek_District "Koibatek District").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012173-12) Colonial authorities created the classification of [Kalenjin people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_people "Kalenjin people"), of which the Tugen were classified as a tribe. The Kalenjin began self-identifying as an ethnicity in the 1950s and 1960s. The Tugen, including politician [Daniel arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_arap_Moi "Daniel arap Moi"), played a large role in creating this identity. Endorois leaders continued to label themselves a subgroup of the Tugen, in part due to their similarity in languages and out of solidarity with Moi.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201228%E2%80%9329-13) After the [independence of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_of_Kenya "Independence of Kenya") in 1963, land controlled by the Native Lands Trust Board was transferred to [county councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_authorities_of_Kenya "Local authorities of Kenya").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201061-10) Endorois land was entrusted to Baringo County on behalf of the Endorois,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011300-5) under the Trust Land Act[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013219-14) and the Constitution of Kenya.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012172-15) The Endorois continued to live on the land[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269-9) until the government of Kenya gazetted Mochongoi Forest as a [game reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_reserve "Game reserve"). The Lake Hannington Game Reserve (later Lake Bogoria Game Reserve) was established in November 1973,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201232-16) of which the Endorois were not informed until 1977.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012173-12) As a result, 400 Endorois families were coerced into leaving the land.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201232Juma2013214-17) They were relocated to a [semi-arid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-arid "Semi-arid") area[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012173-12) where the majority of their livestock did not survive[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016178-18) and potable water was not available.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020507-19) They were also exposed to [cattle raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_raid "Cattle raid") from the [Pokot people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-Mavenjina-3) The community's food supply became reliant on [humanitarian aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarian_aid "Humanitarian aid").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-20) The government developed tourism in the game reserve, constructing roads, [game lodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_lodge "Game lodge"), and a hotel.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011248-21) Remaining Endorois were subject to a 1983 [eviction notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eviction_notice "Eviction notice") labelling their residence as illegal, and some of their houses were burned.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233Juma2013214-22) The eviction took place after [that year's general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_Kenyan_general_election "1983 Kenyan general election").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma201333-23) The Endorois Welfare Management Committee (later the Endorois Welfare Commission; EWC) was created in 1985. Its first chair was Peter Changole, a teacher.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-24) The government refused to recognise the organisation.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011265-25) Endorois leaders met with Moi, by then the [President of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Kenya "President of Kenya"), on 28 December 1994 at Lake Bogoria.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016179-26) He issued a directive for land in the Mochongoi Forest to be re-gazetted and allocated to the Endorois.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-24) According to the EWC, Moi issued the directive a second time in November 1995, but it was not realised either time.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016179-26) Five-acre parcels were created for 312 people in the early 1990s. This was subject to allegations of [land grabbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_grabbing "Land grabbing"); according to a later account by Kiplenge, it was "hijacked by powerful politicians in [Baringo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_District "Baringo District") and [Koibatek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koibatek_District "Koibatek District") districts to settle their own people".[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-24) Endorois protestors led a [barricade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barricade "Barricade") in October and November 1995, blocking the road to Lake Bogoria and calling for land compensation. This led to eleven charges of [unlawful assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unlawful_assembly "Unlawful assembly").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-24) Juma Kiplenge, a lawyer who served as chair of EWC in the 1990s, faced [death threats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_threats "Death threats") and was arrested twice—in August 1996 for leading the unregistered EWC and in 1997 for leading an Endorois Cultural Festival without permission—with poor prison conditions. This gained the attention of [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") which said he had "suffered repeated harassment because he has taken on cases which the authorities do not want pursued" and agreed to take his case. Charles Kamuren, who had served as EWC's secretary since 1985 and would become its president in 2003, was also arrested several times.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233%E2%80%9334-27) ### Judicial cases and aftermath \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Judicial cases and aftermath")\] [![Image 1: Protestors marching with signs with the slogans "Inaction is injustice. Kenya: Endorois & Ogiek's reparations can't wait any longer," and "Time for action, not excuses. Kenya: Start Endorois & Ogiek's reparations now."](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Endorois_%26_Ogiek_Peoples_of_Kenya.jpg/250px-Endorois_%26_Ogiek_Peoples_of_Kenya.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Endorois_%26_Ogiek_Peoples_of_Kenya.jpg) A protest against the Kenyan government's failure to grant land to the Endorois and [Ogiek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogiek "Ogiek") The EWC filed a case against the government in the mid-1990s, alleging that it had failed to share the revenue of Lake Bogoria Game Reserve with the Endorois.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-28) The [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_/(Kenya/) "High Court (Kenya)") at [Nakuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru "Nakuru") dismissed the case in 2002.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-28) It ruled that the removal had been legal under the Trust Land Act[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012174-29) as the establishment of the game reserve superseded the Endorois community's land claim and the government had compensated them.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269-9) It said that Kenyan law did not recognise traditional land claims.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269NdlovuNwauche2022209-30) After [rubies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubies "Rubies") were discovered to the north of Lake Bogoria, the government granted a concession to the Canadian mining company Corby Limited in 2002. In November 2004, the opening of the mine was blocked by protestors. Kamuren said that he received a threatening letter from the District Education Officer days after this protest. The discovery of rubies, along with the discovery of an enzyme used to develop a bleach formula, contributed to feelings among the Endorois that they were being excluded from the wealth of Lake Bogoria.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201234%E2%80%9335-31) The NGOs [Minority Rights Group International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_Rights_Group_International "Minority Rights Group International") and [Cemiride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemiride "Cemiride")—both of which had worked on a pastoralist initiative with the EWC—chose to take the case surrounding Endorois land claims in 2003.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-28) They wrote to the [African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Commission_on_Human_and_Peoples%27_Rights "African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights") (ACHPR) that year, alleging that, in removing the Endorois from their traditional lands, Kenya had violated the Endorois people's rights to [religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion"), [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_science_and_culture "Right to science and culture"), [property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_property "Right to property"), natural resources, and [development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_development "Right to development").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301-32) The ACHPR admitted the case _[Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on Behalf of Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case "Endorois case")_ in 2005.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-28) The ACHPR issued its ruling in 2009,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013213-33) finding Kenya guilty of all violations, and recognising the Endorois as an [indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_people "Indigenous people").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301%E2%80%93302-34) It recommended that Kenya recognise the Endorois community's land claim, grant them complete access to the land, and compensate them for their losses. The Endorois initially anticipated the government would follow these recommendations, but the government took little action.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020510%E2%80%93511-35) [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") listed Lake Bogoria as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") in 2011 despite complaints by the EWC that the Endorois had not been involved.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhatiEpstein2023367-36) In 2013, [Grace Jelagat Kipchoim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Jelagat_Kipchoim "Grace Jelagat Kipchoim") became the first Endorois person elected as a member of parliament for the [Baringo South Constituency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_South_Constituency "Baringo South Constituency").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUdell202346-37) The government began sharing profits from enzyme extraction with the Endorois in 2014.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020511-38) The Kenyan government published the Endorois People's Biocultural Protocol on 31 August 2019,[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022218%E2%80%93220-39) a report on the community's use of resources on their land. The report noted the community's [climate change adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_adaptation "Climate change adaptation") measures; the Endorois had implemented sustainable farming practices such as more diverse and [drought-tolerant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drought-tolerant "Drought-tolerant") crops, as well as destocking and [supplementary feeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_feeding#Types_of_cattle_feeds "Cattle feeding") of livestock. They also supported their culture's environmental values through [ecotourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecotourism "Ecotourism").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBatt2024184-40) UNESCO began including the community in the management of Lake Bogoria in a plan published in 2021.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhatiEpstein2023367-36) However, many Endorois people were removed from [Mukutani Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mukutani_Forest&action=edit&redlink=1 "Mukutani Forest (page does not exist)"), a protected area created by the [Kenya Forest Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Forest_Service "Kenya Forest Service") in 2017 without the community's permission. By 2022, over 10,000 Endorois were relocated from this land to the towns of [Marigat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marigat "Marigat"), [Nyimbei](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyimbei&action=edit&redlink=1 "Nyimbei (page does not exist)"), and [Sandai](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sandai,_Kenya&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sandai, Kenya (page does not exist)"); an individual's request to return to the land in 2024 was denied.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-41) By 2023, Kenya had not granted the Endorois full rights to the land, and the community faced [extreme poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_poverty "Extreme poverty"). Meanwhile, [water level rise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_level_rise "Water level rise") of Lake Bogoria destroyed residential, cultural, and economic sites, including drinking water sources and the lake's only healthcare facility.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUdell202344%E2%80%9345-42) Unauthorised extraction of enzymes from Lake Bogoria also continued, according to Endorois leaders in 2025.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-43) The Endorois are a [clan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan "Clan") of the [Tugen people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tugen_people "Tugen people"), a subgroup of the [Kalenjin people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_people "Kalenjin people").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201229-44) At the time of the Endorois case, their population was 60,000, or 400 families.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInman20148-45) Although the 2019 [Kenya Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenya_Census&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kenya Census (page does not exist)") recorded that there were 45,000 Endorois people, this may have been an undercount.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-Kiburo-46) They speak a variety of the [Kalenjin language cluster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi%E2%80%93Markweta_languages "Nandi–Markweta languages"), most closely related to the [Tugen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tugen_language "Tugen language") and [Keiyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keiyo_language "Keiyo language") languages.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201225-47) As of 2024, the Endorois people live in Kapkun Village, Marigat Division, Baringo South.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-48) The Endorois widely feel a kinship with the rest of the Tugen peoples. Kiplenge described the Endorois as "a subtribe of the Tugen-Kalenjin tribe". Many Endorois people say the community's identification as a distinct indigenous group is for strategic purposes. However, according to Charles Kamuren, the fifth chair of the EWC, the Endorois had always been a distinct group but, until the 1980s, had been convinced otherwise by politicians and Tugen elite.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201229%E2%80%9330-49) [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Lake_bogoria_view.jpg/250px-Lake_bogoria_view.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lake_bogoria_view.jpg) [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria") features in Endorois culture and beliefs. The Endorois people are [pastoralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoralism "Pastoralism") and [semi-nomadic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-nomadic "Semi-nomadic").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268-2) The livelihoods of the Endorois are dependent on the [grazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing "Grazing") of [livestock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livestock "Livestock")—sheep, goats,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012173-12) and [Zebu cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zebu_cattle "Zebu cattle").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-Kiburo-46) Traditionally, this involved herding the animals in Mochongoi Forest during the dry season and the [lowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowland "Lowland") of Lake Bogoria during the wet season.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012173-12) Lake Bogoria is highly culturally valued as livestock feed from its [pastures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasture "Pasture") and [salt licks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_lick "Salt lick").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268-2) This Endorois also traditionally [kept bees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beekeeping "Beekeeping") on this land.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBatt2024183-50) A wild [nightshade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightshade "Nightshade") called _[kisochon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanum_americanum "Solanum americanum")_ was traditionally a major part of Endorois cuisine and was harvested weekly when grains were out of season. _Kisochon_ was eaten as a side dish for [ugali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugali "Ugali") and was also integral to special occasions. However, it has lost popularity due to its bitter taste and has become endangered amid a decrease in soil quality.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-51) The Endorois community is traditionally governed by [elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elder_/(administrative_title/) "Elder (administrative title)").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011265-25) The community is divided into clans, each with a natural phenomenon (such as a plant or animal) as its [totem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totem "Totem").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-Kiburo-46) According to Endorois beliefs, Lake Bogoria is the spiritual home of the Endorois, including the souls of the dead.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305-52) Religious sites exist around the lake.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011255-53) The area is used for a large annual festival and smaller, more frequent ceremonies,[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011255NdlovuNwauche2022210-54) including [funerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral "Funeral"), [weddings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding "Wedding"), [circumcisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumcision "Circumcision"), and [initiations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiation "Initiation"). It also has sites for prayers and [burials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial "Burial").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305-52) Unlike other Kalenjin peoples, the Endorois do not believe themselves to have migrated from elsewhere.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201230-55) Endorois folklore says that Mochongoi Forest was the home of their ancestors[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201231-56) and the location of the first Endorois settlement.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269-9) In the creation of their indigenous identity, the Endorois began referring to the forest as their "birthplace".[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201231-56) 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_ref-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020500_1-0)** [Nasirumbi 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#CITEREFNasirumbi2020), p. 500. 2. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268_2-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268_2-1) [_**c**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268_2-2) [Claridge 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#CITEREFClaridge2019), p. 268. 3. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_ref-Mavenjina_3-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois#cite_ref-Mavenjina_3-1) Mavenjina, Martin (13 December 2017).
