_**Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on Behalf of Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya**_, also known as the **Endorois case**, was a ruling of the [African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Commission_on_Human_and_Peoples%27_Rights "African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights") (ACHPR) surrounding the removal of the [Endorois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois "Endorois") people from [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria") by the [government of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Kenya "Government of Kenya"). The representatives of the Endorois alleged that being removed from their [traditional land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_land_rights "Indigenous land rights") had violated the rights [to culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_science_and_culture "Right to science and culture"), [religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion"), [property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_property "Right to property"), disposal of natural resources, and [development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_development "Right to development"), as defined in the [African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Charter_on_Human_and_Peoples%27_Rights "African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights"). The ACHPR found Kenya responsible for all counts of breaching the charter. The Endorois case was a [landmark decision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmark_decision "Landmark decision") on [indigenous rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_rights "Indigenous rights"), the first international ruling on the right to development, and the first ACHPR ruling on the definition of [peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People "People") or [indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_people "Indigenous people").

The Endorois, a [pastoralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoralism "Pastoralism") community, historically lived around Lake Bogoria. The Kenyan government removed them from this land between 1973 and 1986 for the creation of a [game reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_reserve "Game reserve"), which was later used for tourism and [ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby "Ruby") mining. Despite promises by the government, the Endorois were only partially compensated, and the reserve did not share its revenue with the community. The Endorois Welfare Council (EWC) filed a case against the government with the [High Court of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_/(Kenya/) "High Court (Kenya)") in the 1990s, but the court ruled that the removal had been legal and the Endorois did not have a claim to the land. Considering it infeasible to pursue the case further in Kenyan courts, the EWC sought to file a case with the ACHPR. It was represented by the international NGO [Minority Rights Group International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_Rights_Group_International "Minority Rights Group International") and the Kenyan NGO [Centre for Minority Rights Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Minority_Rights_Development "Centre for Minority Rights Development"), which filed a communication with the ACHPR in 2003, alleging that the removal of the Endorois had violated their rights.

The ACHPR admitted the case in 2005 and heard the case in 2009, issuing its ruling November 2009. The ACHPR ruled that the Endorois were an indigenous people and should be recognised as traditional landowners. It ruled violations of the rights to religion, as the Endorois had lost access to religious sites; property, as Kenya had not recognised Endorois land ownership or provided adequate compensation; natural resources, as the Endorois had the right to use and conserve their land; and development, as developments on the land had lacked the [free, prior, and informed consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free,_prior,_and_informed_consent "Free, prior, and informed consent") of the Endorois.

The ACHPR recommended that the Kenyan government grant the Endorois complete recognition and access to their land, as well as compensation. The government took little action to implement these recommendations, for which it faced disapproval from the ACHPR and [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") bodies. Though the Endorois have been granted limited land access and revenue sharing, they have not been granted full ownership, as of 2023. The Endorois decision influenced other cases involving land rights, such as the [Ogiek case](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ogiek_case&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ogiek case (page does not exist)") against Kenya.

### Relocation of the Endorois

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Relocation of the Endorois")\]

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Lake_bogoria_view.jpg/250px-Lake_bogoria_view.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lake_bogoria_view.jpg)

The Endorois were relocated from [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria").

The [Endorois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois "Endorois") people historically lived as [pastoralists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoralists "Pastoralists") near [Lake Bogoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bogoria "Lake Bogoria") and Mochongoi Forest in western Kenya.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011300Lynch201231-2) The lake is sacred in Endorois culture and was traditionally used for ceremonies.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305-3) The government of [British Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Kenya "British Kenya") granted them [indigenous land rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_land_rights "Indigenous land rights") to the area of Lake Bogoria, which independent Kenya initially continued.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011300%E2%80%93301-4) Under the Trust Land Act,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013219-5) the land was held by the county governments of [Baringo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_County "Baringo County") and [Koibatek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koibatek_District "Koibatek District") on behalf of the Endorois.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012173-6) The Kenyan government held the power to seize the land by [eminent domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain "Eminent domain") or under the terms of the Trust Land Act, which allowed it to "set apart" the land for any purpose without consulting the community.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013219-5)

In November 1973, a [game reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_reserve "Game reserve") was created around Lake Bogoria and 400 Endorois families lost their land. The government said that the each Endorois family would be compensated with 3,150 [Kenyan shillings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_shillings "Kenyan shillings") (about 30 British pounds) and that part of the forest would be set aside for their resettlement.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201232-7) The government also promised that it would construct [cattle dips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_dip "Cattle dip") and [reservoirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reservoir "Reservoir") and that the Endorois would benefit from 25% of revenue and 85% of employment from the game reserve. However, the community did not receive these benefits,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8) and they were not resettled. Only 170 of the families that had been relocated received the promised 3,150 shillings, which were given in 1986.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201232Juma2013223-9) The recipients of this funding had expected it to be for relocation assistance, but the government said it was complete compensation for their land.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBavikatte2014161-10) More Endorois people were removed from the land in 1983 following an [eviction notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eviction_notice "Eviction notice") labelling them as [squatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squatter "Squatter").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-11)

After a meeting with Endorois leaders, President [Daniel arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_arap_Moi "Daniel arap Moi") ordered that land be allocated for the Endorois, and plots were established in the early 1990s; however, there were allegations of [land grabbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_grabbing "Land grabbing"). The Endorois held several protests and community events in following years.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-11) The failure of Moi's plan inspired the Endorois to file a court case.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016179-12)

### Human rights in the African Charter

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Human rights in the African Charter")\]

Kenya is a party to the [African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Charter_on_Human_and_Peoples%27_Rights "African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights"), a treaty of the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union") (AU) overseen by the [African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Commission_on_Human_and_Peoples%27_Rights "African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights") (ACHPR).[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201237-13) Provisions of the African Charter include [freedom of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") (article 8), [right to property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_property "Right to property") (Article 14), [right to culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_science_and_culture "Right to science and culture") (Article 17), right of peoples to "freely dispose of their wealth and natural resources" (Article 21), and [right to development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_development "Right to development") (Article 22).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301Lynch201236-14)

The African Charter protects [people's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_rights "People's rights") but does not include a definition of [peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People "People").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011302-15) It also does not mention [indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_people "Indigenous people") as the concept was not commonly applied to Africa when the treaty was written.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201237-13) A definition of [indigenous peoples of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_Africa "Indigenous peoples of Africa") was popularized by a late-20th-century global movement in which communities self-identified with the label based on a history of [oppression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppression "Oppression") or [marginalisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalisation "Marginalisation").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201226%E2%80%9327-16) Due to this movement, the ACHPR created the Working Group on Experts in Indigenous Populations/Communities (WGIPC) in October 2000 to address the recognition of indigenous peoples of Africa and their rights. This working group defined indigenous peoples using four criteria: "the occupation and use of a specific territory; the voluntary perpetuation of cultural distinctiveness; self-identification as a distinct collectivity, as well as recognition by other groups; and experience of subjugation, marginalization, dispossession, exclusion or discrimination".[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011303%E2%80%93304Lynch201237-17)

Other indigenous rights mechanisms, including the UN's [Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_on_the_Rights_of_Indigenous_Peoples "Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples") (UNDRIP) and jurisprudence of the [Inter-American Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-American_Court_of_Human_Rights "Inter-American Court of Human Rights") (IACtHR), described a [right to traditionally owned lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_land_rights "Indigenous land rights") and resources.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011304,_307Lynch201239-18) Kenya abstained from voting on UNDRIP, and the country's laws did not recognise indigenous rights.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019271%E2%80%93272-19) The ACHPR recognised UNDRIP as a source of law in 2007.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019268-20) By 2010, the ACHPR had not made a decision regarding the application of people's rights to indigenous groups. The first ACHPR case to apply people's rights to a sub-national group had been _[SERAC v. Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SERAC_v._Nigeria&action=edit&redlink=1 "SERAC v. Nigeria (page does not exist)")_ (2001), which had declared the [Ogoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogoni "Ogoni") to be a people.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201237-13) Prior to the Endorois case, this had been the commission's most comprehensive decision about people's rights, although it did not elaborate on what qualifies a group as a people.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDjoyou_Kamga2011387-21) The African Charter is the only human rights instrument to include the right to development.[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-23) By 2010, the ACHPR interpreted the right to development as a people's right that that states must protect, and it had not decided a case about the right.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011302Lynch201236-24) This right was also defined in the UN's Declaration on the Right to Development, which urged states to enable the "active, free and meaningful participation" of humans in their development.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011310-25)

### Pursuit of the case

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Pursuit of the case")\]

#### High Court of Kenya

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: High Court of Kenya")\]

The Endorois Welfare Management Committee (later the Endorois Welfare Council) was created in 1985.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201233-11) In the mid-1990s, the EWC filed the case _William Yatich Sitetalia, William Arap Ngasia et al v Baringo County Council_.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022209-26) The case focused on the government's failed promise to share the revenue of Lake Bogoria Game Reserve with the Endorois.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8) The case was brought to the [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_/(Kenya/) "High Court (Kenya)") at [Nakuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru "Nakuru") in 1998 and was dismissed. This case was brought to the court again in 2000[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowkes2018129-27) and was dismissed in April 2002.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-Mavenjina-28) It ruled that the removal had been legal under the Trust Land Act[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012174-29) as the establishment of the game reserve superseded the Endorois community's land claim and the government had compensated them. The court held that Lake Bogoria was a natural resource and declined to rule on the right to property,[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269-30) stating that the law should not protect land rights based on cultural claims.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019269NdlovuNwauche2022209-31) It also noted that the [Kenyan Bill of Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenyan_Bill_of_Rights&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kenyan Bill of Rights (page does not exist)") protected property rights for individuals but not for groups.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011260-32) The court said, "It is now too late to complain. In any case there is no proper identity of the people who were affected by the setting aside of the land to form the game reserve that has been shown to court".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8)

The EWC appealed their case but considered it unlikely to succeed due to the Kenyan judiciary's inefficiency and lack of clarity about the right to appeal.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201063Ndayambaje2016179-33) After the High Court case, the government continued to sell the lands of Lake Bogoria, granting a [concession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concession_/(contract/) "Concession (contract)") to a ruby mining firm in 2002.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShelton201177-34) This mining posed a risk of [water pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_pollution "Water pollution").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBavikatte2014161-10) The [Kenya National Commission on Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_National_Commission_on_Human_Rights "Kenya National Commission on Human Rights")—an agency created in 2002 after the [National Rainbow Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rainbow_Coalition "National Rainbow Coalition") took power—stated its willingness to participate in discussions with the Endorois about their case.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201240%E2%80%9341-35)

#### Application to ACHPR

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Application to ACHPR")\]

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/IAEA_meeting_with_Abraham_Korir_Sing%E2%80%99Oei%2C_Vienna%2C_June_2025_07.jpg/250px-IAEA_meeting_with_Abraham_Korir_Sing%E2%80%99Oei%2C_Vienna%2C_June_2025_07.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IAEA_meeting_with_Abraham_Korir_Sing%E2%80%99Oei,_Vienna,_June_2025_07.jpg)

[Korir Sing'Oei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Korir_Sing%27Oei "Abraham Korir Sing'Oei") (pictured in 2025) was the legal strategy director of [Cemiride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemiride "Cemiride") when the organisation took the Endorois case.

[Minority Rights Group International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_Rights_Group_International "Minority Rights Group International") (MRG), a British NGO supporting [indigenous rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_rights "Indigenous rights"), first worked with the EWC during a pastoralist initiative led by the [Centre for Minority Rights Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Minority_Rights_Development "Centre for Minority Rights Development") (Cemiride), a Kenyan NGO. In 2003, MRG took applications for a case with the ACHPR, and the legal strategy director of Cemiride, [Korir Sing'Oei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Korir_Sing%27Oei "Abraham Korir Sing'Oei"), suggested the Endorois case. The head of law of MRG, Cynthia Morel, said the case was noteworthy due to the Endorois community's strong coordination and their specific claim over land not claimed by other groups.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8) The case filed with the ACHPR was different from the one in the High Court, rather than appealing the case.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012174-29)

Cemiride, supported by MRG and the [Centre for Housing Rights and Evictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Centre_for_Housing_Rights_and_Evictions&action=edit&redlink=1 "Centre for Housing Rights and Evictions (page does not exist)"), filed a [letter of intent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_of_intent "Letter of intent") on 22 May 2003.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd2010Djoyou_KamgaFombad2013208-36) Cemiride and the MRG alleged that the Kenyan government had illegally expelled the Endorois people from their land. According to this communication, the Endorois people were divided, which violated their [cultural integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cultural_integrity&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cultural integrity (page does not exist)");[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-38) relocated to semi-arid land, which denied them access to religiously, culturally, and economically important locations; and excluded from government decisions to sell the land, use it for tourism development, and grant [concessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concession_/(contract/) "Concession (contract)") to ruby mining companies. Cemiride and the MRG alleged that the acts violated the African Charter's rights to culture, religion, property, disposal of natural resources, and development.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301-39) This communication cited the ACHPR's ruling in _SERAC v. Nigeria_[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012175-40) and focused on recently developed jurisprudence of indigenous rights.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201075-41) The Endorois sought the [remedies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_remedy "Legal remedy") of restitution of their land and financial compensation.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013215-42)

The complainants petitioned to admit the case in August 2003.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201063-43) Kenya argued that the Endorois case was ineligible for the ACHPR as there were further options within the national court system, with the case being pending at the [Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Appeal_of_Kenya "Court of Appeal of Kenya").[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016180-44) The commission sided with the complainants, who said such options would be ineffective,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012176-45) noting that Kenyan law did not recognise collective rights.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201066Ndayambaje2016179-46) Another eligibility requirement was that alleged acts must have occurred after the ratification of the African Charter, as it did not apply retroactively. Although the removal of the Endorois had occurred before Kenya's ratification, the case was admitted under an exception for continuing violations.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201065-47)

The case was subject to [provisional measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_measure_of_protection "Provisional measure of protection") in 2004,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201213-48) and Kenya followed the ACHPR's order to terminate ruby mining on Lake Bogoria.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201066%E2%80%9367-49) The case was admitted in 2005.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8) The hearing of the case was delayed for three years as the Kenyan government did not meet the ACHPR's deadlines.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301%E2%80%93302Bavikatte2014162-50) The ACHPR heard the case during its 41st session[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301%E2%80%93302-51) and published its decision during its 46th session[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDjoyou_KamgaFombad2013208-52) in May 2009,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8) before issuing its ruling in November 2009[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013213InmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018407-53) and ratifying it on 2 February 2010.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201235-8)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-Mavenjina-28) The commission ruled in favor of the Endorois[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201225-54) and found the Kenyan government responsible for all violations.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301%E2%80%93302-51) The commission's decision cited jurisprudence from African and other human rights mechanisms.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTETalbot2017182-55)

### Preliminary questions

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Preliminary questions")\]

The commission's discussion of the case began by describing whether the Endorois were a people, as applied to the African Charter, and whether they were indigenous.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011302-15)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-56) Kenya argued that the Endorois were not a people as they were one of four clans of the [Tugen people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tugen_people "Tugen people"), in turn a subgroup of the [Kalenjin people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_people "Kalenjin people"),[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305Lynch201225-57) and that "modern society" had caused them to lose their unique culture.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMennenMorel201277Tamuno2017329-58)[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-59) The ACHPR disagreed and said, "the Endorois consider themselves to be a distinct people, sharing a common history, culture and religion."[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305Lynch201238-60)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-61) It drew on precedent in which it had declared groups including the Ogoni, [Katangese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katangese "Katangese"), and [Black Mauritanians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haratin "Haratin") to be peoples.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011302-15) The commission also ruled that the Endorois were indigenous due to the value they placed on their traditional land.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305-3)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-62) In addition to citing the WGIPC's definition,[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu201137Gilbert2011253-63) the commission's definition of indigenous peoples drew from international precedent, including that of the IACtHR,[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-66) as well as UNDRIP.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu201139Lynch201239Claridge2019272-67)

### Rights to religion and culture

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Rights to religion and culture")\]

After ruling that the Endorois were an indigenous people, the ACHPR ruled that their cultural practices qualified as a religion.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012178-68) Its definition of the right to religion was based on the African Charter as well as General Comment 22 of the [United Nations Human Rights Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council "United Nations Human Rights Council"), which states that the concept is "to be broadly construed".[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018409-69)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-70) The EWC alleged that the removal of the Endorois from Lake Bogoria had violated the rights to religion and culture as the lake was integral to the community's religion and its pastoralist culture. Kenya argued that the removal had occurred in accordance with laws, which made it acceptable under an exception listed in Article 8 of the Charter. The commission denied this, as states are not allowed to invoke exceptions listed in the African Charter, and stated that Kenya did not have a reasonable legal justification to limit the right to religion.[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-71) The commission noted that Article 17 requires states to provide for "the conservation, development and diffusion of culture" without mentioning exceptions.[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-72) It said that the stated goal of creating a nature reserve did not necessitate the removal of the population.[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-73) It ruled that the right to culture had been violated as Lake Bogoria was integral to Endorois culture,[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013230-74) and they had lost access to sites associated with their beliefs[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011305%E2%80%93306-75) while being relocated to semi-arid land cut them off from natural resources vital to their agricultural practices.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011257-76)[\[j\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-77)

The complainants argued that Endorois land was the property of the community as the Trust Land Act and the [Constitution of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Kenya "Constitution of Kenya") had granted recognition of their land claims.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013218-78)[\[k\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-79) In deciding on whether the right to property had been violated, the ACHPR formulated a description of property rights for indigenous peoples.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011307-80)[\[l\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-81) Although the African Charter does not list an explicit [right to land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_land "Right to land"),[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011249-82) the commission determined that indigenous lands constitute property,[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011307-80) based on cases such as _SERAC v. Nigeria_ and _[Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Malawi_African_Association_and_Others_v._Mauritania&action=edit&redlink=1 "Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania (page does not exist)")_, which had applied property rights to require the protection of land claims.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011307Murphy2012180-83)[\[m\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-84) Although Kenya argued that the country had no laws protecting traditional land claims, the ACHPR held that the absence of such law violated property rights.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInman201413-85) It stated that traditional ownership is equivalent to legal ownership and that governments must protect indigenous groups' ownership of lands rather than merely grant them access to them.[\[n\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-86) The commission also held that traditional ownership applies only to resources traditionally used by a group, based on precedent from the IACtHR. Thus, rubies were not a traditional resource of the Endorois, although ruby mining still violated their land rights as it impacted other resources.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011307%E2%80%93308-87)[\[o\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-88)

According to Article 14, limitations on property rights must be "in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with ... appropriate laws".[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011308Lynch201238-89)[\[p\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-90) Kenya argued that the removal of the Endorois had been legal (as the government had authority over trust land), that the government had granted them adequate access to their land,[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011308%E2%80%93309Gilbert2011259-91) and that it had been in the [public interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_interest "Public interest") as the goal had been nature conservation.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013220-92)[\[q\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-93) The commission held that the requirement for "general interest" was heightened in the case of indigenous peoples due to the importance of their property.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011308Lynch201239-94) It ruled that Kenya's trust land system had not protected the right to property,[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013220-92) that forcing the removal of the Endorois had violated the requirement of legality,[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShelton2012219-95) and that it had been [disproportionate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportionality_/(law/) "Proportionality (law)") to the government's goal.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201238Juma2013220-96)[\[r\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-97) It also stated that Kenya had not adequately negotiated with the Endorois before limiting their access to the land, which would have required full consent.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011308Lynch201239-94)[\[s\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-98) The commission noted that, according to UNDRIP, indigenous peoples had a right to repatriation or compensation for their land.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019272%E2%80%93273-99)[\[t\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-100) It stated that the financial compensation given to the Endorois was inadequate and "\[flew\] in the face of common sense and fairness".[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011309Juma2013223-101)[\[u\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-102)

### Right to resources and right to development

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Right to resources and right to development")\]

Kenya argued that it had not violated the Endorois's right to resources as the county governments had used their wealth from the game reserve for local developments that the Endorois could still access. However, the commission held that a people had the right to use the resources in its land, as decided in _SERAC v. Nigeria_.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012185-103)[\[v\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-104) The commission considered the right to resources and its connection to the right to property, meaning that an act violating the right was required to be in the public interest.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTETalbot2017179-105) It ruled that Kenya had violated this right as they had limited the community's ability to gain wealth from their land.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy2012185%E2%80%93186-106)[\[w\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-107) It stated that the goal of creating a nature reserve could have been done with the involvement of the Endorois, who, being from the land, would be "best equipped to maintain its delicate ecosystems", and did not pose a threat to conservation.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011308%E2%80%93309MennenMorel201279Shelton2012220-108)[\[x\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-109)

The ACHPR formulated a definition of the right to development in this case. It described the right as "both constitutive and instrumental", meaning it was subject to tests of both [procedural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procedural_law "Procedural law") and [substantive law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substantive_law "Substantive law").[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011309Djoyou_Kamga2011390Lynch201239-110)[\[y\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-111) Kenya argued that its developments on Endorois land were beneficial to the Endorois. The commission agreed but ruled that it was not enough to protect their rights.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShelton201179-112) It said, "The result of development should be empowerment of the Endorois community."[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011Lynch201239Juma2013226-113)[\[z\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-114) The commission's discussion of this right addressed the concepts of [free, prior, and informed consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free,_prior,_and_informed_consent "Free, prior, and informed consent") and [freedom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_choice "Freedom of choice"),[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022212-115) and stated that development required consultation with and consent of communities.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011310-25)

Kenya argued that the community had sufficiently been involved in consultations with mining companies, but the commission sided with the complainants, who argued that the representatives in consultations had not been chosen by the community itself. It noted that the Kenyan government had refused to register the EWC[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011265-116) and that the Endorois community members involved in discussions had been [illiterate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illiterate "Illiterate")[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011310-25) and "were informed of the impending project as a [fait accompli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fait_accompli "Fait accompli")".[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011310Djoyou_Kamga2011382-117)[\[aa\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-118) It also disagreed with Kenya's argument that indirect participation through the democratic system was sufficient involvement.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgenthauReisch2020111-119)[\[ab\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-120) The commission also held that the right to development requires development to benefit the people.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011310Lynch201239-121) It said that the Kenyan government had instead caused damage by removing the Endorois people's access to resources necessary for development.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011310-25)[\[ac\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-122)

### Conclusion and remedies

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Endorois_case&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Conclusion and remedies")\]

The ACHPR concluded, "by restricting access to Lake Bogoria, \[the respondent state\] has denied the community access to an integrated system of beliefs, values, norms, mores, traditions and artefacts closely linked to access to the Lake".[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011306Lynch201238-123)[\[ad\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-124) It called for the Kenyan government to recognise Endorois ownership over their traditional land, return them to this land with unrestricted access, give them compensation and royalties for their losses, recognise the EWC,[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-126) hold discussions with the Endorois on the implementation of these remedies, and report on this implementation within three months.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011311Juma2013231-127)[\[ae\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-128) These directions did not specify a timeline or describe how to delineate the land of the Endorois.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201069Juma2013224-129) While the commission called for projects on Endorois land to pay royalties to the community, it did not require these projects to stop.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoshoff202230-130)

The Endorois community hailed the decision as a victory. An Endorois individual, Cheptoroi, said, "That the scary days are gone seems too good to be true."[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301-39) A celebration was held by Lake Bogoria on 20 March 2010. Festivities included rituals performed by elders and the slaughter of cattle and goats.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011300-131) Kenya's [Minister for Lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Minister_for_Lands_\(Kenya\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Minister for Lands (Kenya) (page does not exist)"), [James Orengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Orengo "James Orengo"), spoke at the celebration at Lake Bogoria, saying, "The government has no option but to implement the African Commission's recommendations."[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011311Lynch201241-132) He said he would write to the [Cabinet of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Kenya "Cabinet of Kenya") ensuring the decision's implementation.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018414-133)

African indigenous groups celebrated the Endorois case as a victory.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoraDanielKlugman201765-134) Several minority groups in Kenya, as well as elsewhere in Africa and Latin America, asked the chair of the EWC, Charles Kamuren, to consult them on cases.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201241-135) Cemiride took cases from other Kenyan peoples that had land disputes: the [Ogiek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogiek "Ogiek"), who faced eviction from the region of [Mau Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Forest "Mau Forest") and [Mount Elgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon "Mount Elgon"), and the [Nubians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubians "Nubians"), who claimed [Kibera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibera "Kibera") as an ancestral homeland.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201241-135) Human rights groups celebrated the decision's support of indigenous rights, and they placed pressure on the government of Kenya amid other concerns of human rights violations by the country.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-136) Commentators including the Endorois expected the Kenyan government to follow the ACHPR's recommendations.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020510-137)

[![Image 4: Protestors marching with signs with the slogans "Inaction is injustice. Kenya: Endorois & Ogiek's reparations can't wait any longer," and "Time for action, not excuses. Kenya: Start Endorois & Ogiek's reparations now."](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Endorois_%26_Ogiek_Peoples_of_Kenya.jpg/250px-Endorois_%26_Ogiek_Peoples_of_Kenya.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Endorois_%26_Ogiek_Peoples_of_Kenya.jpg)

February 2024 protest against the Kenyan government's failure to grant land to the Endorois and [Ogiek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogiek "Ogiek")

The ACHPR did not have the power to enforce its decisions,[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201240Murphy2012188-138) and the government of Kenya had little political will to enforce the Endorois recommendations.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020510-137) The government did not follow the recommendation delivering a report within three months.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020511-125) The ACHPR and activists such as the Endorois influenced the drafting of the 2010 Constitution of Kenya, which reformed the land law to recognise community ownership.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMennenMorel201282Inman201418-139) In January 2011, Member of Parliament [Ekwee Ethuro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekwee_Ethuro "Ekwee Ethuro") asked Orengo why he had not taken action as he had stated; Orengo replied that the government could not yet implement remedies because it had not received a sealed copy of the ruling. The government did not take action after receiving such a copy.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018414-133) During the session of the WGIPC later that year, Kenya's [Ministry of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ministry_of_Justice_\(Kenya\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ministry of Justice (Kenya) (page does not exist)") stated it would act toward implementation.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018415-140) By 2013, the land remained in the control of the park service, which had control over the Endorois people's access to the land.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuma2013232-141) Meanwhile, some members of the Endorois community voiced disapproval of the EWC for its failure to hold elections or report its finances.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201241-135)

The government of Kenya acted to delay the implementation of the Endorois decision.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowkes2018130-142) Kenya applied for Lake Bogoria Game Reserve to be a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site "UNESCO World Heritage Site") without the involvement of the Endorois,[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019273-143) facing protests from the EWC and other activist groups.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarreiro_Carril2016231-144) The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) also evaluated it as a natural site without acknowledging the Endorois or the case.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhatiEpstein2023367-145) The ACHPR issued resolutions calling for UNESCO and IUCN to review their processes to protect indigenous rights,[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019273BhatiEpstein2023367-146) stating that listing the World Heritage Site without the consent of the Endorois violated their right to development.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarreiro_Carril2016231-144) The Kenyan government met with the ACHPR at its headquarters in April 2013 to discuss a plan for implementation of the Endorois decision. Kenya's representative said the plan would be published within three months, but this did not occur.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamuno2017330%E2%80%93331InmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018415-147) At the ACHPR's 53rd session, WGIPC held a workshop about the decision, which was attended by Endorois leaders but not Kenyan officials.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInmanSmisCirimwamiBahalaokwibuye2018416-148) In November 2013, the ACHPR issued a resolution against Kenya calling for implementation.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020511-125) This was the first time it had issued a resolution against a state for non-compliance.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowkes2018130-142)

MRG wrote to the African Commission in August 2014, calling for this non-compliance to be referred to the AU, but received no response.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamuno2017331-149) Other groups joined the EWC to put pressure on the Kenyan government, including the [Kenya Human Rights Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Human_Rights_Commission "Kenya Human Rights Commission") and the Economic Social and Cultural Rights Network.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoraDanielKlugman201766-150) The administration of [Uhuru Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Kenyatta "Uhuru Kenyatta") established a task force for the matter in September 2014,[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoraDanielKlugman201766Fowkes2018130-151) but it did not include any Endorois people and only held one meeting with the community. The task force was not renewed[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020511-125) and did not result in action.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowkes2018130-142) Bodies of the UN stated disapproval of Kenya's lack of action in 2016 and 2017. In response, the KWS issued a memorandum recognising Endorois land claims.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowkes2018130-142) By 2017, the EWS was working with the Colombian human rights organisation Dejusticia, which had worked on other indigenous rights cases.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-Mavenjina-28)

The Endorois received some financial concessions: the [Kenyan Wildlife Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Wildlife_Service "Kenyan Wildlife Service") (KWS) negotiated with the biotechnology firm [Biozymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Biozymes&action=edit&redlink=1 "Biozymes (page does not exist)") in 2014 to pay the Endorois for the right to process enzymes found in Lake Bogoria; Baringo County later agreed to share 10% of the nature reserve's revenue; and the reserve employed some members of the community.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasirumbi2020511-125) The government published the Endorois People's Biocultural Protocol on 31 August 2019. It discussed the situation of the Endorois and their land rights, noting the importance of the Endorois case in recognising these rights. This protocol outlined the process of negotiation with the Endorois, legal use of resources on their land, and benefit-sharing.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022218%E2%80%93220-152) As of 2023, Kenya has not officially returned the land to the Endorois or compensated them.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUdell202344-153) About sixty members of the Endorois and Ogiek communities led a march in Nairobi on 6 February 2024, submitting a letter of demands to the [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General_of_Kenya "Attorney General of Kenya"). They protested the lack of action to implement the Endorois case and the ongoing removal of the Ogiek.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-154)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-155)

The Endorois case was the most comprehensive ruling the ACHPR had yet made.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201225-54) It received coverage by academics[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUdell202344-153) and was considered an example of [strategic litigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_litigation "Strategic litigation").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBatt2024170-156) Commentators have called it a [landmark case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmark_case "Landmark case") on indigenous rights in Africa.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2011246Inman20149-157)

The Endorois case was the first decision in which the ACHPR made a ruling on the definition of indigenous peoples[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011301%E2%80%93302-51) or recognised indigenous rights.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTELynch201226-158) It made a direct ruling on the African Charter's definition of peoples, unlike the previous Ogoni case, which had only implicitly recognised the Ogoni as a people with a right to land.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDjoyou_KamgaFombad2013213MorgenthauReisch2020101-159) The Endorois case was one of the first indigenous rights cases after the creation of UNDRIP,[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201082-160) although the decision relied on the African Charter rather than UNDRIP.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTESing'OeiShepherd201086Murphy2012189-161) The case set a precedent that protection of indigenous rights required granting peoples ownership of their traditional lands, not only access.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetersmann2021141-162) The case also held that the right to culture is a collective right, which had not previously been established in international law and would later be agreed by the IACtHR.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurvis2013482%E2%80%93483-163)

It was the first decision by any international body to rule on the right to development.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshamu2011302Lynch201226-164)[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-166) It established a standard for development, requiring free, prior, and informed consent from the landowning people.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDjoyou_Kamga2011390-167) It was the first ruling to state that this requirement applied to any developments affecting a community, whereas the IACtHR had more narrowly applied it to large projects.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurvis2013482%E2%80%93483-163)

The Ogiek people filed [a land dispute case](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ogiek_case&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ogiek case (page does not exist)") with the [African Court of Human and People's Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Court_of_Human_and_People%27s_Rights "African Court of Human and People's Rights"), which heavily relied on the Endorois decision.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetersmann2021142-168) The Ogiek cited the decision in the Endorois case that required states to protect the development of peoples.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClaridge2019276-169) The Endorois case was also cited by the complainants in _Abdalla Rhova Hiribae v. Attorney General_, a Kenyan High Court case in which peoples residing by the [Tana River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tana_River_/(Kenya/) "Tana River (Kenya)") alleged violations of their right to development. The court ruled against them, arguing that, unlike with the Endorois, adequate consultation had occurred.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022222%E2%80%93223-170)

The rulings of the Endorois and Ogiek cases both provided precedent in international human rights law.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016176-171) They were the first cases in the African human rights system to recognise traditional ownership as legal ownership,[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgenthauReisch2020103%E2%80%93104-172) and they established a requirement of free, prior, and informed consent for development within Kenyan law.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022202-173) The ACHPR's opinion in the Endorois case was reflected in the National Guidelines for Free, Prior, and Informed Consent, written by the [Ministry of Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ministry_of_Environment_\(Kenya\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ministry of Environment (Kenya) (page does not exist)") in 2016.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdlovuNwauche2022217-174)

Although the case did not address the [right to a healthy environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_a_healthy_environment "Right to a healthy environment") (Article 24 of the African Charter), the ruling indirectly protected this right for the Endorois.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTENdayambaje2016184%E2%80%93185-175) The rulings of the Endorois and Ogiek cases established a view that indigenous peoples can drive environmental protection.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorois_case#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgenthauReisch2020108-176)

Nature of the Case
------------------

Complaint against Kenyan government alleging violations under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the Constitution of Kenya and international law, for the forced removal of the Endorois peoples from their ancestral lands; Violation of Land and Natural Resource Rights; Violation of Indigenous Rights; Freedom of Religious and Cultural Practices; Right to Development.

Summary
-------

In the 1970s, the Kenyan government evicted hundreds of Endorois families from their land around the Lake Bogoria area in the Rift Valley to create a game reserve for tourism.  The Endorois, an indigenous people, had been promised compensation and benefits, but these were never fully implemented, and the community’s access to the land was restricted to the discretion of the Game Reserve Authority. This prevented the community from practicing their pastoralist way of life, using ceremonial and religious sites, and accessing traditional medicines. Complainants (Centre for Minority Rights Development, Kenya and Minority Rights Group International on behalf of the Endorois Welfare Council) submitted this claim before the African Commission on Human Rights after domestic legal efforts and action failed to constitute an effective remedy for the violations alleged.

The Commission found that the Kenyan government had violated the Endorois’ rights to religious practice, to property, to culture, to the free disposition of natural resources, and to development, under the African Charter (Articles 8, 14, 17, 21 and 22, respectively). The Commission stated that lack of consultation with the community; the subsequent restrictions on access to the land; and the inadequate involvement in the process of developing the region for use as a tourist game reserve, had violated the community’s right to development under the U.N. Declaration on the Right to Development. Also, the Commission found that the Kenyan Government’s Trust Land System violated the Endorois’ right to property. The system allowed gradual encroachment onto Endorois land, and even though the system allowed for compensation, it nevertheless violated property rights by effectively causing forced evictions.  For these violations, the Commission recommended that the government recognize rights of ownership, restitute to the Endorois’ their ancestral lands, compensate their losses, and ensure the Endorois benefit from the royalties and employment opportunities within the game reserve.

**Keywords:** Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on behalf of Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya, 276/2003, Development

Enforcement of the Decision and Outcomes
----------------------------------------

The Commission’s decision was formally approved by the African Union at its January 2010 meeting.  The Commission’s decision calls upon the state to report on the implementation of its recommendations within three months from the date of notification and further recommends collaboration with the Endorois in implementing these remedies. Concurrently with this decision, Kenya is undergoing a process of Constitutional review and there is hope on the part of civil society involved in this case that its result will positively impact the negotiation process in favor of greater recognition of economic, social and cultural rights.

Significance of the Case
------------------------

This case marks the first time the Commission has recognized indigenous peoples’ rights over traditionally owned land and their right to development under the African Charter. The decision is also noteworthy because the Commission emphasizes the African Charter’s protection for collective claims to land rights by indigenous communities. It is also a relevant decision for economic, social and cultural rights advocates because the Commission stated that while the Kenyan Constitution guaranteed civil and political rights, it did not give an equivalent degree of constitutional protection to economic, social, cultural, or group rights and concluded that this denied the Endorois an opportunity to launch an effective claim on their ancestral land in the Kenyan High Court.

Groups Involved in the Case

![Image 1](https://www.witness.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/CE64FB67-CB30-43BC-93E1-33502E6CF497-214x300.jpeg)

### **The Kenyan Government Must Face up to its obligations to the Endorois Community**

The repeated failure by the Kenyan government to implement the decision of the African Commission on Human and People’s Rights in the Endorois case deepens decades of inequality, neglect and abuse.

On April 4 2022 WITNESS together with a coalition of NGOs advocating for the full implementation of the Endorois decision by the African Commission on Human and People’s rights issued a report today on the non implementation of the decision twelve years after. The coalition which is made up of WITNESS, Centre for Minorities Right Development (CEMIRIDE), Endorois Welfare Council (EWC) and Minorities Rights Group International (MRG), released the report which documents how the loss of the Endorois ancestral land has led to a vicious cycle of impoverishment and underdevelopment of the community.

In the 1970s, the Endorois, Indigenous Peoples in Kenya, were evicted from their ancestral land in and around Lake Bogoria to pave the way for the creation of a national park and tourist facilities. This was done without consultation or adequate and effective compensation for the community. In 2003, the Endorois community through the Centre for Minority Rights Development, Minority Rights Group and with support from WITNESS filed a complaint with the Africa Commission. In a landmark decision, the African Commission in 2009, concluded that the Endorois eviction from their Indigenous land violated their human rights. This decision was upheld by the African Union in 2010, setting a major legal precedent by recognising for the first time in Africa, Indigenous peoples’ rights over traditionally owned land and their right to development.

Twelve years after the African Commission’s decision, the situation has only worsened as the Kenyan government’s refusal to implement the decision has left the Endorois people desolate and in extreme poverty. The devastating human cost of a tourist destination is the lived experience of the Endorios people. Although the Lake Bogoria area is endowed with natural resources and continues to yield substantial revenue, the Endorois are yet to reap its benefits and their displacement has resulted in poor access to amenities such as healthcare, clean water, and education. The Endorois, including women and children, have to walk long distances(as far as 24 kilometres) to fetch water. The only other alternative is to buy water – an expense most community members cannot afford.

_“It’s possible to spend Ksh500 ($5) in one day on water. And many of us just rely on our_ _animals. We don’t have any other work. So, water is many times a luxury.” – Madam_ _Fancie Kiprotich, a member of the Endorois Women’s Forum_

The registration of the Endorois Welfare Council (EWC) is the only recommendation of the African Commission’s decision that has been fully implemented. Two other recommendations – around the payment of royalties and the provision of unrestricted access to Lake Bogoria and surrounding areas – have seen tokenistic implementations. There is an inextricable link between the collective land rights of Indigenous peoples, and their right to self-driven development. The ownership, use, control over and the management of land, all directly affect the enjoyment of a wide range of socio-cultural and economic rights.

_“The lack of implementation of regional decisions by the Government of Kenya continues_ _to cast a shadow on progressive litigation recognizing the land rights of indigenous_ _communities” – Eunice Olembo, Africa Legal Officer, Minority Rights Group International –_ _Africa Office._

The adoption of the Community Land Act in 2016, is a significant step forward for securing Indigenous communities’ land rights in Kenya, however, the lack of implementation calls to question the political will of the Kenyan government to prioritize the protection of Indigenous peoples’ rights in the country.

_“We take note and applaud the Kenyan government for finally acknowledging the_ _existence of Indigenous peoples in Kenya. We thus expect that the government should_ _move with speed to ensure that Indigenous communities, starting with the Endorois,_ _secure their rights to land. For indigenous peoples, realisation of their land rights is_ _critical, if their food security, as envisioned in the United Nations Declaration on the_ _Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas (UNDROP) is to be_ _achieved. Government should thus implement the recommendations of the UN Universal_ _Periodic Review (UPR) which include implementation of the Africa Commission’s_ _Decision on the Endorois.” – Nyang’ori Ohenjo, Executive Director, Centre for Minority_ _Rights Development._

Kenya cannot effectively fight poverty and the associated problems of illiteracy, unemployment and poor health if a significant proportion of its population is poor. A true commitment to the protection of the Indigenous people in Kenya demands that the government fulfills its obligation under the international and national laws that it is bound by. The report puts forward the following recommendations:

**Recommendations**

1\. The government should constitute a new task force on the implementation of the African Commission’s Endorois Decision. The composition of the task force should include representation of the Endorois and Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Experts.

2\. The National Land Commission, according to Section 15 of the National Land Commission Act, 2012, read together with Article 2 (5) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, should adopt and fully implement the Endorois decision.

3\. The government should immediately facilitate the development of an inventory/register of Indigenous peoples in Kenya and hence protect their lands.

4\. Government should pass benefit-sharing legislation as required by the Constitution of Kenya 2010.

5\. Endorois benefit-sharing mechanisms and structures should be expanded to include the representatives of the EWC.

6\. The government should provide data on internally displaced persons because of ethnic conflicts, climate change and development projects and ensure that their rights and issues are adequately addressed.

7\. The African Commission on Human and Peoples Rights (ACHPR) should step up its efforts to engage with the Kenyan Government on the implementation of its decision on the Endorois complaint.

8\. Donors and development actors should support capacity building of government officers in charge of the implementation of the rights of marginalized communities to enable them to understand the importance and value of securing the rights of Indigenous communities in national government development.

9\. CEMIRIDE, WITNESS and MRG and other civil society groups should support advocacy efforts of the Endorois community to implement the African Commission’s decision.

Help us amplify calls for justice for the Endorois by joining our online campaign that is also meant to increase the visibility of the [Endorois Report](https://www.witness.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/Endorois-Report.pdf). Use the #Implement276 or #Justice4Endorois across social media.

[![Image 1: The University of Arizona Wordmark Line Logo White](https://cdn.digital.arizona.edu/logos/v1.0.0/ua_wordmark_line_logo_white_rgb.min.svg)](https://www.arizona.edu/ "The University of Arizona homepage")

[![Image 2: Indigenous Rights and Protected Areas | Home](https://indigenous.arizona.edu/sites/default/files/LAW%20IPLP%20Logo.png)](https://indigenous.arizona.edu/ "Indigenous Rights and Protected Areas | Home")

**INDIGENOUS RIGHTS & PROTECTED AREAS**  
INITIATIVE

Main navigation
---------------

1.  [Home](https://indigenous.arizona.edu/)
2.  Centre For Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International On Behalf of Endorois Welfare Council V. Kenya, 276/2003

African Commission and Court on Human and Peoples Rights

Relevant paragraphs, or extracts

**Decision on Merits**

144\. The present Communication alleges that the Respondent State has violated the human rights of the Endorois community, an indigenous people, by forcibly removing them from their ancestral land, the failure to adequately compensate them for the loss of their property, the disruption of the community's pastoral enterprise and violation of the right to practice their religion and culture, as well as the overall process of development of the Endorois people.

145\. Before addressing the articles alleged to have been violated, the Respondent State has requested the African Commission to determine whether the Endorois can be recognised as a ‘community’ / sub-tribe or clan on their own. The Respondent State disputes that the Endorois are a distinct community in need of special protection. The Respondent State argues that the Complainants need to prove this distinction from the Tugen sub-tribe or indeed the larger Kalenjin tribe. The immediate questions that the African Commission needs to address itself to are:

146\. Are the Endorois a distinct community? Are they Indigenous Peoples and thereby needing special protection? If they are a distinct community, what makes them different from the Tugen sub-tribe or indeed the larger Kalenjin tribe?

147\. Before responding to the above questions, the African Commission notes that the concepts of “peoples” and “Indigenous Peoples / communities” are contested terms. As far as “Indigenous Peoples” are concerned, there is no universal and unambiguous definition of the concept, since no single accepted definition captures the diversity of indigenous cultures, histories and current circumstances. The relationships between Indigenous Peoples and dominant or mainstream groups in society vary from country to country. The same is true of the concept of “peoples.” The African Commission is thus aware of the political connotation that these concepts carry. Those controversies led the drafters of the African Charter to deliberately refrain from proposing any definitions for the notion of “people(s).” In its Report of the Working Group of Experts on Indigenous Populations/Communities,48 the African Commission describes its dilemma of defining the concept of “peoples” in the following terms: Despite its mandate to interpret all provisions of the African Charter as per Article 45(3), the African Commission initially shied away from interpreting the concept of ‘peoples’. The African Charter itself does not define the concept. Initially the African Commission did not feel at ease in developing rights where there was little concrete international jurisprudence. The ICCPR and the ICESR do not define ‘peoples.’ It is evident that the drafters of the African Charter intended to distinguish between the traditional individual rights where the sections preceding Article 17 make reference to “every individual.” Article 18 serves as a break by referring to the family. Articles 19 to 24 make specific reference to “all peoples.”

148\. The African Commission, nevertheless, notes that while the terms ‘peoples’ and ‘indigenous community’ arouse emotive debates, some marginalised and vulnerable groups in Africa are suffering from particular problems. It is aware that many of these groups have not been accommodated by dominating development paradigms and in many cases they are being victimised by mainstream development policies and thinking and their basic human rights violated. The African Commission is also aware that Indigenous Peoples have, due to past and ongoing processes, become marginalised in their own country and they need recognition and protection of their basic human rights and fundamental freedoms.

149\. The African Commission also notes that normatively, the African Charter is an innovative and unique human rights document compared to other regional human rights instruments, in placing special emphasis on the rights of “peoples.” It substantially departs from the narrow formulations of other regional and universal human rights instruments by weaving a tapestry which includes the three “generations” of rights: civil and political rights; economic, social, and cultural rights; and group and peoples’ rights. In that regard, the African Commission notes its own observation that the term “indigenous” is also not intended to create a special class of citizens, but rather to address historical and present-day injustices and inequalities. This is the sense in which the term has been applied in the African context by the Working Group on Indigenous Populations/Communities of the African Commission. In the context of the African Charter, the Working Group notes that the notion of “peoples” is closely related to collective rights.

150\. The African Commission also notes that the African Charter, in Articles 20 through 24, provides for peoples to retain rights as peoples, that is, as collectives. The African Commission through its Working Group of Experts on Indigenous Populations/Communities has set out four criteria for identifying Indigenous Peoples. These are: the occupation and use of a specific territory; The African Charter is not an accident of history. Its creation by the OAU came at a time of increased scrutiny of states for their human rights practices, and the ascendancy of human rights as a legitimate subject of international discourse. For African states, the rhetoric of human rights had a special resonance for several reasons, including the fact that post-colonial African states were born out of the anti-colonial human rights struggle, a fight for political and economic self-determination and the need to reclaim international legitimacy and salvage its image .

151\. The African Commission is thus aware that there is an emerging consensus on some objective features that a collective of individuals should manifest to be considered as “peoples”, viz: a common historical tradition, racial or ethnic identity, cultural homogeneity, linguistic unity, religious and ideological affinities, territorial connection, and a common economic life or other bonds, identities and affinities they collectively enjoy – especially rights enumerated under Articles 19 to 24 of the African Charter – or suffer collectively from the deprivation of such rights. What is clear is that all attempts to define the concept of Indigenous Peoples recognize the linkages between peoples, their land, and culture and that such a group expresses its desire to be identified as a people or have the consciousness that they are a people.

152\.
